title: Memory Mosaics at scale

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'removing long-term memory from Memory Mosaics v2 after training degrades the performance on the RULER question-answer tasks by 20%~30%.' However, Table 10 reports with/without long-term memory scores of 58.9→38.5 (4k), 55.5→22.2 (8k), 54.9→20.0 (16k), 53.4→20.2 (32k), which correspond to relative degradations of 34.6%, 60.0%, 63.6%, and 62.2% respectively (absolute point drops of 20.4, 33.3, 34.9, 33.2). Under no natural reading — relative or absolute — do the printed numbers support the claimed '20%~30%' degradation; the smallest relative drop is 34.6% and only the 4k absolute drop (20.4 points) is near the claimed range. The magnitude of the effect is materially understated relative to the paper's own table.

Equation (9) reuses the symbol v-tilde (ṽ_T / \tilde{v}_T) for BOTH the raw projection (\tilde{v}_T = W_ψ x_T) and the smoothed value on the left-hand side of the averaging equation (ṽ_T = γ \tilde{v}_T + (1−γ)\tilde{v}_{T+1}). As printed, substituting \tilde{v}_T = W_ψ x_T into the smoothing equation forces W_ψ x_{T+1} = W_ψ x_T (i.e., v_T = v_{T+1}) for γ ≠ 1, making the equation self-referential and mathematically incoherent. The key extractor in Equations (7)-(8) uses a distinct symbol (breve k) for the smoothed quantity, and the original Memory Mosaics paper uses a distinct symbol for the smoothed value; the v2 equation collapsed that distinction. The intended fix is obvious (a distinct symbol for the smoothed value), but the displayed equation is internally contradictory as written.

summary: Verification of 'Memory Mosaics at scale' (uncertainty mode, lenient strictness) covered all 10 equations, 13 tables, all sections, citations, and cross-section consistency. The core mathematical claims are sound: the kernel-regression-to-attention reduction in Eq. (4) is algebraically correct when all keys share a common squared norm (up to absorbing a factor 2 into the learnable bandwidth β); the adaptive-bandwidth schedule β = β_1 n^α + β_0 in Eq. (6) is consistent with the MISE-optimal rate 1/√β ∝ n^{-1/(p+4)} (β grows with n, so α ∈ (0,1) is correct); and the short/long-term memory overlap condition m < h in Section 3.3 is correct. All Table 1/2/9 benchmark averages were recomputed and match; Table 4's '12.3% to 14.8%' and Table 5's '6.5%' gaps match; Tables 3 and 12 are mutually consistent; and the abstract's claims align with the body (persistent-knowledge parity, 12.3–14.8% new-knowledge gains, >10% ICL gains). Two findings are reported: (1) a data-reporting inconsistency in Appendix G — the text claims long-term-memory removal degrades RULER QA by '20%~30%' while Table 10 shows 34.6%–63.6% relative degradation (confidence 0.8); (2) a self-referential notation collision in Eq. (9), which reuses ṽ for both the raw value projection and the smoothed value (confidence 0.7). Minor issues noted but not elevated to findings: the Section 5.2 claim '1.4%~5.6%' has a lower bound that should be 1.6% per Table 3; the 'novel theoretical insight' that normalized-key Gaussian-kernel associative memory equals softmax attention is well-known prior art (e.g., kernel/attention unification literature) and is better framed as a reformulation; the in-text citation year [Beck et al., 2025] disagrees with the reference list (NeurIPS 2024); and the duplicated example 'tom-and-jerry'/'tom-and-jerry' appears to be a typo. None of these are conclusion-invalidating, but the Table 10 magnitude claim should be corrected or the table recomputed.
